issues.legal_issue: Direct contractual documents and payment acknowledgments outweigh an unexplained failure to object to a rent figure stated incidentally in separate litigation.
material_facts: The lease recorded a monthly rent rate, and the tenants admitted executing it.
The tenants’ letter enclosing rent payments stated that payments were being made at the rate recorded in the lease.
In separate family litigation, a different rent figure was stated incidentally; the landlord did not object, but rent payable was not in issue there.
The appellate authority relied on the incidental statement and found a lower rent rate, and the High Court declined to interfere in revision.
issues.conclusion: The lease and the tenants’ payment letter established the rent rate recorded in the lease; the contrary finding was perverse and ought to have been set aside in revision.
issues.legal_principle: An admission is a piece of evidence whose value depends on the circumstances in which it was made and to whom; it is not conclusive unless it amounts to an estoppel. A mere failure to object is not stronger than an admission. The court weighed the tenants’ direct documentary admissions against the landlord’s failure to object to an incidental, undisputed statement in separate litigation, and held that the contrary appellate finding was perverse.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning eviction for non-payment of rent.
predicates.lease_records_a_rent_rate: The parties’ lease records a particular rent rate.
predicates.tenant_payment_documents_acknowledge_tha: The tenant’s payment documents acknowledge payment at the rate recorded in the lease.
predicates.contrary_rate_appears_only_in_incidental: A different rent rate appears only in an incidental statement in separate litigation, and the landlord’s failure to object there was not an admission on a contested issue.

issues.definition: When an eviction appeal involves a lease and tenant payment documents supporting a rent rate, an incidental uncontested contrary statement does not displace that direct evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A rent controller must provisionally assess disputed arrears, interest, and application costs before requiring the tenant to tender the assessed amount.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding alleged default in rent, and the parties disputed the rent rate and the amount due.
The tenants tendered an amount with interest and costs, but the Rent Controller found it insufficient and ordered eviction.
The statute required payment or tender of arrears, interest, and application costs but did not expressly provide a mechanism for resolving a genuine dispute over the amount before tender.
The Court considered that an interpretation requiring a tenant to tender whatever the landlord claimed would risk eviction despite a genuine dispute.
issues.conclusion: The proviso requires the Controller to make an interim or provisional assessment of the arrears, interest, and application costs, including resolving the disputed rent rate or other matters necessary to quantify them, before the tenant is required to pay or tender the amount on the first hearing after that assessment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 13(2)(i) and its proviso of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, the words “assessed by the Controller” qualify the arrears, interest, and application costs. The provision must be construed to make it workable, avoid hardship and injustice, and advance its tenant-protective purpose. The Court considered the approach to “rent due” in Rullia Ram Hakim Rai v. Fateh Singh and Khadi Gram Udyog Trust v. Shri Ram Chandraji Mandir, and rejected the simplistic approach in Dial Chand v. Mahant Kapoor Chand. It also relied on the equitable principle in Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act and the general interpretive principle of resolving statutory ambiguity in a just and workable manner.

predicates.rent_control_default_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground of non-payment of rent under a rent-control process.
predicates.tenant_disputes_the_amount_or_rate_of_re: The tenant disputes the amount of arrears or the rent rate on which the arrears depend.
predicates.statutory_payment_requirement_does_not_p: The governing payment requirement does not expressly specify how the disputed amount must be determined before tender.

issues.definition: If a tenant disputes the rent amount in a rent-control default proceeding and the payment requirement supplies no prior dispute-resolution mechanism, the Controller must first provisionally quantify the payment due.

issues.legal_issue: After the tenant pays or tenders the provisionally assessed amount, the Controller must continue to determine the actual arrears where the parties’ dispute remains unresolved.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding involved a dispute over the rent rate and arrears.
The Court directed that the Controller first make a provisional assessment and that the tenant then pay or tender the assessed amount on the first hearing after the assessment.
The Court specified that, after compliance, the Controller should determine the dispute through a summary inquiry based on the parties’ pleadings.
issues.conclusion: If the tenant complies with the provisional assessment, the Controller must continue the proceeding and finally adjudicate the dispute over arrears.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 13(2)(i) requires provisional assessment followed by payment or tender on the first hearing after the assessment. Compliance does not itself resolve the parties’ underlying dispute: the Controller must conduct a summary inquiry and make a final adjudication. The meaning of the first hearing follows Mam Chand Pal v. Shanti Agarwal: it is the date on which the court applies its mind to the facts and controversy, not merely the date for filing a written statement.

predicates.rent_control_default_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground of non-payment of rent under a rent-control process.
predicates.controller_made_provisional_assessment: The Controller provisionally assessed the arrears, interest, and application costs.
predicates.tenant_paid_or_tendered_assessed_amount: The tenant paid or tendered the amount provisionally assessed by the Controller.

issues.definition: When the tenant pays or tenders the provisional assessment in a rent-control default proceeding, the Controller must continue to determine the disputed arrears.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to comply with the Controller’s provisional assessment requires an eviction order.
material_facts: The Court prescribed a provisional assessment of arrears, interest, and application costs, followed by an opportunity for the tenant to pay or tender that amount.
The Court stated that if the tenant fails to comply with the provisional assessment, nothing remains to be done and an eviction order follows.
issues.conclusion: If the tenant fails to pay or tender the amount provisionally assessed, an eviction order must follow.
issues.legal_principle: Under the procedure the Court derived from the proviso to Section 13(2)(i), the Controller first quantifies the amount payable by an interim or provisional order. The tenant must pay or tender that amount on the first hearing after the assessment; on failure to comply, eviction follows.

predicates.rent_control_default_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground of non-payment of rent under a rent-control process.
predicates.controller_made_provisional_assessment: The Controller provisionally assessed the arrears, interest, and application costs.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_pay_or_tender_assessed_: The tenant did not pay or tender the amount provisionally assessed by the Controller.

issues.definition: If a tenant in a rent-control default proceeding does not pay or tender the provisional assessment, an eviction order follows.

issues.legal_issue: A difference between the provisional assessment and the final determination requires adjustment, and a final shortfall may be cured before eviction.
material_facts: The Court contemplated that the final determination could match, exceed, or fall below the amount provisionally assessed.
It held that a tenant who complied with the provisional order should not be evicted immediately merely because the final determination found a shortfall.

The Controller may give a reasonable opportunity to pay or tender the deficit, and may consider whether the tenant regularly paid or tendered rent falling due during the proceeding when exercising that discretion.
issues.conclusion: If the final amount is less than the provisional amount, the Controller may direct a refund of the excess; if it is greater, the Controller may make a conditional eviction order giving the tenant a reasonable opportunity to pay or tender the deficit, with compliance preventing eviction. The tenant’s payment conduct during the proceeding is a relevant factor in deciding whether to allow that opportunity.
issues.legal_principle: The procedure under Section 13(2)(i) and its proviso permits the Controller to reconcile the provisional assessment with the final adjudication. If the tenant deposited too much, the Controller may order a refund. If the deposit is deficient, the Controller may make a conditional eviction order allowing a reasonable time to cure the deficit, relying on the Controller’s statutory discretion and principles of equity and fair play. The tenant’s payment or tender of rent during the proceeding is relevant to that discretion.

predicates.rent_control_default_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground of non-payment of rent under a rent-control process.
predicates.tenant_complied_with_provisional_assessm: The tenant paid or tendered the amount provisionally assessed by the Controller.
predicates.final_arrears_differ_from_provisional_as: The final adjudication finds that the arrears differ from the amount provisionally assessed.

issues.definition: If a compliant tenant’s final arrears differ from the provisional assessment, the Controller adjusts an excess or allows a reasonable opportunity to cure a deficit before eviction.

issues.legal_issue: An eviction order made without the required provisional assessment is vitiated and the proceeding must be reconsidered under the prescribed procedure.
material_facts: The Rent Controller ordered eviction after finding that the tenants’ tender was deficient, but had not made a provisional assessment of the arrears, interest, and application costs under the procedure set out by the Court.
The Court set aside the orders of the Rent Controller, the Appellate Authority, and the High Court and remitted the proceeding for a provisional order and a fresh decision.
issues.conclusion: Because no provisional assessment had been made, the eviction order was vitiated; the matter was remanded for the Controller to hear the parties, make a provisional assessment, allow the tenants an opportunity to pay or tender, and decide the case afresh under the stated procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(i) and its proviso require the Controller to assess provisionally the arrears, interest, and application costs before requiring the tenant to pay or tender the amount. An eviction decision reached without that required procedural step is vitiated. The Court remanded the matter for the Controller to follow the procedure it established.

predicates.rent_control_default_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground of non-payment of rent under a rent-control process.
predicates.controller_ordered_eviction_without_prov: The Controller ordered eviction without first provisionally assessing the arrears, interest, and application costs.

issues.definition: An eviction order made without a provisional assessment in a rent-control default proceeding is vitiated, and the proceeding must be reconsidered after that assessment.
